topics.name: PCP theorem
topics.description: Polynomial-time verification with logarithmic randomness and a constant number of proof-bit queries characterizes NP.

topics.name: Polynomial distance
topics.description: The Schwartz–Zippel bound limits the fraction of points where a nonzero polynomial vanishes.

topics.name: Low-degree extension
topics.description: Interpolation represents a table on a grid by a unique polynomial with a degree bound in each variable.

topics.name: Labels and encoding
topics.description: Polynomial labels turn field values and their polynomial expressions into bits and distinguish full, affine and homogeneous observations.

topics.name: Verifier and query trees
topics.description: A verifier selects an adaptive query tree from its input and random seed, with explicit acceptance probabilities and proof-address bounds.

topics.name: Polynomial-time implementation
topics.description: A finite multi-stack machine implements the verifier or witness checker with polynomial running time.

topics.name: Colouring constraints
topics.description: Vertex values and edge differences satisfy polynomial equations exactly when they define a proper three-colouring.

topics.name: Vanishing certificates
topics.description: A polynomial vanishing on a grid admits a decomposition using the coordinate vanishing polynomials and a certificate expressed by two identities.

topics.name: Linearity and self-correction
topics.description: Linearity testing finds a nearby linear word, and two randomly shifted queries recover a requested value with controlled error.

topics.name: Queries, randomness and repetition
topics.description: Query counts, fair-bit sampling, proof length and independent repetition give the resource bounds and final soundness error.

topics.name: Proof tables and checks
topics.description: Four pairs of points and lines tables supply the answers read by four low-degree tests, two grid tests and a difference check.

topics.name: Binary low-degree test
topics.description: Small rejection gives one polynomial whose encoding is close to the points table on both full and homogeneous labels.

topics.name: Zero-on-grid test
topics.description: Corrected certificate queries test vanishing identities at prescribed points and relate failure on the grid to rejection.

topics.name: Completeness and soundness
topics.description: An honest colouring passes every check, while sufficiently small rejection forces four nearby polynomials to describe a proper colouring.

topics.name: Reduction to three-colouring
topics.description: Accepting computations become finite constraints, Boolean clauses and graphs while preserving the existence of a witness.

topics.name: NP witness verification
topics.description: A language belongs to NP when membership is witnessed by a polynomial-length string accepted by a polynomial-time checker.

topics.name: Standard low-degree test
topics.description: Weighted interpolation at generator powers tests low degree, with plurality correction turning small rejection into polynomial agreement.

topics.name: Local correction over fields
topics.description: Random line queries recover a polynomial value at a prescribed point or bound the probability of accepting a wrong value.

topics.name: Bivariate agreement
topics.description: Agreement between low-degree row and column polynomials produces a nearby bivariate polynomial and consistent values at selected crossings.

topics.name: Point-versus-line test
topics.description: Agreement with supplied line polynomials at random points yields one nearby polynomial of bounded total degree.

topics.name: Set-multilinear encoding
topics.description: Writing exponents in a fixed number of base digits replaces a line polynomial by a polynomial of fixed total degree.

topics.name: Hadamard test
topics.description: Linearity, unit, product and affine consistency checks test whether a word is close to the encoding of one field value.

topics.name: Inner low-degree test
topics.description: A random choice between Hadamard testing and a binary weighted identity tests one encoded line entry for low degree.

topics.name: Local correction on bits
topics.description: Weighted bit queries and tests of encoded line entries recover a homogeneous observation at a prescribed point, allowing rejection.

passages.quote:

comparisons.note: The quote first describes rejection by an ideal polynomial test. The formal statement instead bounds rejection of the actual two-corrector test after allowing errors in nearby polynomial encodings; its lower bound depends on $D$, $h$, $q$, both distances and the correction constant.

passages.quote:
Perfect completeness
supplies such bits on yes-instances and soundness excludes them on
no-instances, all in polynomial time, so the problem is in NP.

comparisons.note: The formal statement puts the language in NP for the same concrete machine model, assuming a polynomial-time verifier, exact logarithmic randomness, a polynomial proof-address bound, perfect completeness and soundness error $1/2$. These are the properties assumed in the paragraph.

passages.quote:
Encodings of

is a nonzero **linear functional**, a map $x\mapsto s'\cdot x$ with

comparisons.note: For any two distinct binary messages, the formal statement says their homogeneous linear encodings have relative distance exactly $1/2$. This is the distance claim justified in the quote by pairing zeros and ones.

PCP.np_subset_pcp.text: For a language $\mathcal L$ in NP, the formal statement supplies one polynomial-time verifier, constants $\alpha,\beta,\ell$ and a polynomial $p$, all fixed independently of the input. On length $n$ it uses exactly $\alpha\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil+\beta$ fair bits and makes at most $\ell$ proof queries, each below $p(n)$. A yes-instance has one proof accepted for every seed; every proof of a no-instance has acceptance probability at most $1/2$. Proofs are represented by indefinitely indexed bits, but only the polynomially bounded initial segment can affect the verdict.

PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorGrid.constraints.text: For a polynomial $\chi$ and a graph on $H^m$, the formal statement equates vanishing of $\chi^3-1$ on $H^m$ and of $\widehat E(x,y)((\chi(x)-\chi(y))^3-1)$ on $H^{2m}$ with the corresponding equations at vertices and edges. This equivalence holds over any field. It does not itself turn a solution into a three-colouring. The interpretation as the colours $1,\omega,\omega^2$ uses the characteristic-two field containing $\mathbb F_4$ fixed earlier in the exposition.

PCP.Algebraic.GridVanishing.vanishesOn_i.text: A polynomial vanishes on the finite grid $H^m$ exactly when it is a sum $\sum_j Q_j(X)Z_H(X_j)$ with bounded coefficient polynomials. The formal statement works over any integral domain and gives $\deg Q_j\leq\max(\deg P-|H|,0)$. The preceding decomposition result retains the more informative inequality $\deg Q_j+|H|\leq\deg P$ whenever $Q_j\ne0$. That qualification matters for zero quotients and for input degree below $|H|$. The identities concern polynomials, rather than only sampled values.

PCP.Algebraic.PointLineTest.exists_close.text: Let $f$ be any field-valued table, and supply one polynomial of degree at most $d$ for every indexed line. If $q\geq10^6d^3$ and the point-versus-line test rejects with probability $\delta\leq1/(4\cdot10^6)$, some polynomial of total degree at most $d$ differs from $f$ on at most a $2\delta$ fraction of points. The comparison parameter is uniform over all of $F$, including zero. No consistency between the supplied line polynomials is assumed, and the statement also covers degree zero.

PCP.Algebraic.GeneratorLowDegreeTest.exi.text: Choose a generator $\zeta$ of the finite field's nonzero elements and the interpolation nodes $\zeta,\ldots,\zeta^{c+1}$. Assume $q>2c$. If the weighted interpolation test rejects at most a fraction $\delta<1/[2(c+2)^2]$ of the uniform pairs $(u,v)$, its table is within $2\delta$ of a polynomial of total degree at most $c$. The formal statement needs neither characteristic two nor a separately assumed nearby polynomial. Its conclusion is about total degree, not merely the degree in each variable.

PCP.Algebraic.BLR.exists_linearMap_dista.text: The domain is a finite-dimensional binary vector space, and the received word can be arbitrary. If the fraction of pairs $(a,b)$ violating $h(a+b)=h(a)+h(b)$ is at most $\varepsilon$, the formal statement supplies a linear functional at relative distance at most $\varepsilon$. There is no restriction requiring $\varepsilon$ to be small. The conclusion is existence of a nearby linear functional; it does not yet say that the word is evaluation of the nonlinear labels at a single message.

PCP.Algebraic.Hadamard.test_soundness.text: For full labels of degree at most $r\geq1$, rejection at most $\delta<1/28$ gives one binary message. Its degree-$r$ encoding is within distance $\delta$ of the received word. Restricting that same word to all affine labels gives distance at most $3\delta$ from the same message's affine encoding. Constants are included in the affine domain. This statement therefore supplies more than BLR linearity: it identifies evaluation at a message and controls two different averages.

PCP.Algebraic.Hadamard.testQueries_lengt.text: The formal statement counts $2r+4$ entries in the query list for every seed and every label degree $r\geq1$. At $r=3$ this is ten. Answers shared between the linearity, unit, affine-consistency and product checks are reused. The list includes two extra positions for each of the $r-1$ product checks. This is a query-list length, not a claim that every seed visits $2r+4$ distinct addresses, and it makes no assertion about the different eight-query test in the original paper.

PCP.Algebraic.EncodedLineLowDegreeTest.e.text: Work in a finite characteristic-two field with binary coordinates, positive base $b$, label degree at least one, and the stated interpolation and correction nodes. Put $D=cb^c$. Under $q\geq10^6D^3$ and $J\kappa\leq1/(4\cdot10^6)$, the formal statement produces one polynomial of total degree at most $D$. Its encoding is within $S\kappa$ of the points table both on full labels and on homogeneous linear labels, averaging over points in each case. The lines table is arbitrary; no separate promise of its closeness is required. The statement also permits $c=0$ with the same node conditions.

PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.rejecti.text: Fix the characteristic-two field, its binary coordinates, generator test nodes, valid correction nodes, and an element of order three for the colours. Let $H$ be nonempty, $h=|H|$, $D=cb^c$, with $c,b\geq1$. The formal statement assumes $q\geq10^6D^3$, $100Dh\leq q$ and $m(h-1)\leq D$. Every eight-table proof for a non-three-colourable graph on $H^m$ then has rejection probability at least $g(c)$. The gap depends on the fixed inner degree, not the graph size. Appendix A meets these hypotheses.

PCP.Lang.ThreeColorRuntime.polyTimeAlg.text: The formal statement certifies the implemented amplified graph verifier's step algorithm on a concrete finite machine. Given the input, random bits and previous proof answers, that algorithm either produces the next proof address or returns a decision in polynomial time in their encoded length. The fixed query bound then gives polynomial running time for the verifier. This is the efficiency result used in the final PCP theorem; the separate probability and resource statements alone would not establish machine running time.

PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.exists_.text: A three-colourable graph on $H^m$ supplies an eight-table proof with rejection probability zero. The hypotheses include a characteristic-two field with an element of order three, nonempty $H$, distinct interpolation nodes, valid correction nodes, positive digit base, and the degree-capacity inequality $5m(h-1)<b^c$. The proof tables encode a colouring extension, its difference polynomial and the two vanishing certificates. Since the verifier samples uniformly from a finite nonempty seed space, zero rejection means every seed accepts this one proof.

PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalCorrection.fail.text: At each fixed target $a$, the failure event includes both rejection and returning a bit different from $L(P(a))$. Assume $q>2c$, the generator and correction nodes, positive base $b$, $\deg P\leq D$, $cb^c\leq D$, and homogeneous distance at most $\delta$ for the points table. The bound is $C\kappa_a+\delta+D/[2(q-1)]$. The probability averages over the homogeneous label and all other random choices. No closeness promise for the lines table, no smallness bound on $\kappa_a$, and no guarantee for each fixed label is asserted.

PCP.Algebraic.BinaryZeroOnGridCorrection.text: Suppose $P$ fails to vanish on nonempty $H^m$, both $P$ and its proposed certificate $M$ have total degree at most $D$, and $cb^c\leq D$. With $q>2c$ and the prescribed nodes, let $\delta_P,\delta_M$ bound the two received tables' homogeneous distances. The actual grid test has rejection at least $((1-Dh/q)/2-\delta_P-2\delta_M-D/(q-1))/(1+2C)$. The lines tables may be arbitrary. The denominator is positive, but the whole lower bound need not be positive until the field and error budgets are imposed.

PCP.pcp_subset_np_concrete.text: This is the reverse inclusion for the same concrete machine model used in the forward theorem. Assume that the verifier has a polynomial-time step algorithm, randomness exactly $\alpha\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil+\beta$, queries restricted to a polynomial initial segment, perfect completeness and soundness error $1/2$. The formal statement places its language in NP. The witness is the relevant finite proof prefix, and exhaustive checking uses polynomially many seeds. The actual theorem concerns that fixed computation model, rather than assuming a separate abstract cost model exists.

PCP.Algebraic.Hadamard.relativeDistance_.text: For two different binary messages $s$ and $s^{\prime}$, exactly half of the homogeneous linear labels distinguish them. Equivalently, the words $x\mapsto s\cdot x$ and $x\mapsto s^{\prime}\cdot x$ have relative distance $1/2$. This is a statement about the entire label domain, so it also gives the probability of detecting inequality with one uniform label. It is not a statement that every label distinguishes the messages, and it does not assume the received words are merely close to honest encodings.

PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorAmplifiedVerifie.text: For the fixed positive repetition count $R$ chosen from the rejection gap, the amplified graph verifier has query budget $187R$ and randomness exactly $32000000R\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil+32000000R$. It retains the polynomial proof-address bound, perfect completeness and soundness error $1/2$. All these properties concern one verifier. The statement does not itself establish polynomial running time, the NP reduction, the numerical value $R=1137847282503168$, or the unamplified gap $1/R$; those require their own definitions and supporting results.

PCP.Algebraic.Hadamard.linearEncode.text: A binary message $s$ determines the word $h_s(x)=\sum_i s_i x_i$ over $\mathbb F_2$. Each position $x$ specifies one homogeneous linear observation of the message, with no constant term. This is the encoding used when a uniform label must distinguish two unequal field values through their binary coordinates. It differs from the affine-label encoding, which also includes constant terms, and from the full degree-three label domain used for the colouring table.

PCP.Reduction.FiniteBooleanConstraints.c.text: For each relation and each binary pattern $p$, the formal definition creates prefix flags and clauses enforcing $z_0=0$, the updates $z_{i+1}=z_i\lor(x_i\mathbin{\mathrm{xor}}p_i)$, and $R(p)\lor z_k=1$. Every update contributes the three OR-gate clauses. The initial and final conditions each contribute one clause, padded with false where necessary. The definition supplies the actual clauses for a family of relations; correctness and the size bound are separate statements, so defining the clauses alone does not assert that the whole NP reduction is efficient.

PCP.Reduction.FiniteBooleanConstraints.o.text:
Under any assignment, the three clauses $(z\lor
eg u)$, $(z\lor
eg v)$ and $(
eg z\lor u\lor v)$ hold together exactly when $z=u\lor v$. The formal statement allows literals, including negations and constants, in all three positions. Short clauses have an extra false literal so that every clause has three positions. This is an equivalence for one OR gate, which supplies the local step used in the prefix-flag construction.

PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.Proof.text: The formal definition allows arbitrary bits in eight tables: points tables for $\chi$, $\chi^{\prime}$, $M_V$ and $M_E$, together with one encoded lines table for each. The first two points tables use degree-three labels and the certificate points tables use affine labels. Every lines table uses affine labels after the set-multilinear encoding. Their domains reflect the $m$, $2m$ and $4m$ field coordinates in the paper. These domains do not promise that the received bits encode polynomials or satisfy any colouring condition.

PCP.Algebraic.SetMultilinear.evaluationP.text: The point $\Phi(z)$ has a coordinate for each of the $c$ digit positions and each of the $b$ possible digit values. At coordinate $(i,j)$ it places $z^{jb^i}$. Coordinates for digit zero therefore equal one, including when $z=0$. The definition supplies the substitution point only. Recovering $p(z)$ from the encoded polynomial additionally needs its degree to be strictly below the capacity $b^c$.

PCP.Algebraic.SetMultilinear.eval_encode.text: Assume the digit base $b$ is positive and $\deg p<b^c$. The formal statement says that evaluating the set-multilinear encoding at $\Phi(z)$ recovers $p(z)$ for every $z$. No exclusion of zero is needed. The strict capacity bound prevents different powers from sharing the same retained digit pattern. The identity actually works over any commutative semiring; the finite field in the exposition is one setting in which it applies.

PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalCorrection.run.text: The formal definition first tests the chosen encoded line entry. It then corrects that entry at $\Phi(z)$ for a nonzero comparison parameter and compares the result with the points-table bit at $a+zv$. If both checks pass, it returns the correction at $\Phi(0)$; otherwise it rejects. The comparison and return use the same inner slope and homogeneous label. The procedure can receive an arbitrary lines table; the graph verifier separately ensures reuse of its tested certificate lines tables.

PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.BranchS.text: The formal definition assigns random choices to seven checks in this order: colour low degree, vertex-certificate low degree, difference low degree, edge-certificate low degree, vertex vanishing, edge vanishing and difference consistency. The last uses two field points and a homogeneous label; the other checks require their own testing and correction choices. This describes their sample spaces. It is not an acceptance rule and does not assert that only one of the seven checks is sampled.

PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.branchT.text: For a chosen one of the seven checks, the formal definition evaluates its acceptance rule on its own random choices. The four low-degree checks read their respective points and lines tables. The two grid checks use those same certificate lines tables, with a self-corrected cubic observation of the colour or difference table. The edge observation also uses the public adjacency extension. The remaining check compares the difference table with the two colour-table values. A separate definition combines all seven verdicts.

PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.test.text: The formal definition combines the seven individual checks by conjunction: the verifier accepts exactly when every check accepts on its supplied random choices. A complete sample contains a seed for each check. This matters for the soundness bookkeeping, since any rejection by one check is also rejection of the combined verifier. There is no factor of seven from selecting one check at random. The definition itself does not establish a rejection gap or polynomial running time.

PCP.Algebraic.SetMultilinear.totalDegree.text: The formal statement bounds the encoded polynomial's total degree by $c$ for every input polynomial, even one exceeding the intended capacity $b^c$. This degree bound alone does not assert set-multilinearity or recovery of the original polynomial. The one-variable-per-digit-group property is proved separately, while the evaluation identity requires input degree strictly below $b^c$. Keeping those three claims separate avoids mistaking a low-degree polynomial for a faithful encoding of an arbitrary high-degree input.

PCP.Algebraic.SetMultilinear.encode.text: The formal definition replaces a power of the original variable by a product selecting one variable from each digit group, then extends that operation linearly across the polynomial's coefficients. It is defined for all input polynomials. Only inputs of degree strictly below $b^c$ are guaranteed to be recovered by the substitution $\Phi$: exponents outside this range can have the same retained $c$ base-$b$ digits. Its availability on a larger domain is therefore not a larger faithful encoding capacity.

PCP.Algebraic.Hadamard.homogeneousIndex.text: This formal definition places a homogeneous linear label $L$ inside the full degree-at-most-$r$ label domain, assuming $r\geq1$. It uses only degree-one monomials and gives the constant term coefficient zero. Thus the homogeneous labels used in the distance and correction bounds are linear observations, not arbitrary degree-$r$ polynomials without a constant term. For $t$ message coordinates there are $2^t$ such labels, compared with $2^{t+1}$ affine labels.

PCP.Algebraic.Hadamard.relativeDistance_.text: Suppose each table value is represented injectively by its binary coordinates and labels have degree at least one. The formal statement says that the relative distance between the two fully encoded tables is exactly half the relative distance between the original tables. The encoded distance averages jointly over the table position and the full label domain. This identity concerns two honest encodings; it does not turn a small full-label error in an arbitrary received table into a homogeneous-label error bound.

PCP.Algebraic.Hadamard.TestRandomness.text: A Hadamard test sample contains two full labels, one affine label, and a separate factor of each degree $j$ with $1\leq j<r$. Sampling uniformly from their product makes these choices independent. The same first full label is reused for the self-corrections, and the same affine label is used in all product comparisons. Consequently the test runs all the listed product checks but saves queries by reusing some answers; the choices of labels and the query positions are distinct objects.

PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.validAu.text: The vertex grid check receives the very same encoded lines table attached to $M_V$ in the eight-table proof. At target $a$ and slope $v$, this formal definition selects its entry indexed by $(a,v)$. It creates no second certificate table and imposes no promise that the received entry is correct. This identity of tables is what lets the soundness analysis combine the low-degree check and local correction for one nearby certificate polynomial.

PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.properA.text: The edge grid check receives the same encoded lines table attached to $M_E$ in the eight-table proof. Its target has four blocks of field coordinates: two for the vertex pair and two for the vanishing-certificate variables. The formal definition selects that table's entry at the requested target and slope. It does not posit a second, independently honest table. The coordinate grouping in the edge constraint is changed separately, without replacing the received certificate data.

PCP.Verifier.CanonicalRandomness.text: The randomness budget is exactly $\alpha\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil+\beta$ for all input lengths $n$, with fixed natural-number constants. This is more specific than an asymptotic bound. It makes the number of fair bits a fixed computable function of input length; a verifier needing fewer bits can ignore the excess. The main theorem provides such constants for each language. This definition alone asserts neither efficient computation of the verifier's decisions nor a bound on its proof queries.

PCP.QueryTree.text: A decision tree of depth at most $\ell$ may stop before making any query or ask one proof bit and continue according to its answer. Its depth bounds the number of bits read on a run, including repeated requests to the same address. It is an upper bound, not a requirement to make exactly $\ell$ reads. The tree contains both possible continuations at every query, so its possible-address set covers all proof answers, not just one execution.

PCP.QueryTree.ofStep.text: Starting from the answers already obtained, the formal definition unfolds a decision rule into a tree with at most $\ell$ further proof queries. If the rule returns a decision, the tree stops. If it requests another query after the budget is exhausted, the tree rejects. The query bound is therefore enforced by construction. This does not assert that the unrestricted decision rule would halt within the budget; that distinction matters when comparing the resulting tree with the verifier's tree.

PCP.Verifier.ImplementedBy.text: For every input and seed, the formal definition requires the tree generated by the algorithm from an empty answer history, with query budget $\ell$, to equal the verifier's tree. The random index is first converted to its fixed-length bit string. Equality covers the query addresses and both continuations at every answer. It compares computation after the budget cutoff: an additional query request causes rejection. It does not independently assert that the unrestricted step algorithm always halts within $\ell$ queries.

PCP.NPCertificate.text: The formal definition packages a polynomial witness bound, a Boolean witness checker, and the statement that membership is equivalent to existence of a bounded witness accepted by that checker. It also requires the checker to satisfy the supplied notion of polynomial time. This is a definition of what evidence for NP membership consists of. In the main theorem, polynomial time is fixed to a concrete finite-machine model, so an arbitrary interpretation of efficiency is not being used to prove the PCP theorem.

PCP.Algebraic.EncodedLineLowDegreeTest.l.text: The formal definition sets $J=2((c+1)K+29)$, where $K$ is the inner decoding constant. This factor converts the binary test's rejection bound into a field-valued point-versus-line rejection bound. It depends only on the fixed inner degree $c$. The binary low-degree theorem requires $J\kappa\leq1/(4\cdot10^6)$ before applying the point-versus-line theorem; the definition of $J$ is not itself a proximity statement.

PCP.Algebraic.EncodedLineLowDegreeTest.s.text: The formal definition sets $S=28+J$, using the line-error factor $J$. The binary low-degree soundness theorem multiplies the actual rejection rate by $S$ to bound both full-label distance and homogeneous-label distance to one polynomial encoding. The constants depend only on $c$. The two distances average over different sets of labels; their sharing the same numerical bound does not identify those sets or make a full-label bound sufficient by itself.

PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalCorrection.soun.text: The formal definition sets $C=2+2(c+1)K$, where $K$ is the inner decoding constant. It accounts for the two corrected reads and direct rejection terms in the local-correction failure estimate. For fixed inner degree $c$ it is independent of the target and graph size. In the theorem, it multiplies the actual rejection rate $\kappa_a$; the separate homogeneous-distance and polynomial-root terms must still be added.
